turns.content: Just got off shift. Ten hours wrestling spiral duct in this heat, I'm wrecked. Toby and the guys posted Lake Chelan pictures today. I wasn't asked. Wednesday's the drop deadline for Mateo's duckpin bowling league, and I don't know if I can make it.

Sounds like a long, brutal one — ten hours of spiral duct in that heat is real work, and coming home to a feed full of lake pictures you weren't in stings in a specific way. That's a fair thing to feel.

On the bowling: the deadline is Wednesday, so you've got a couple of days. The honest question is whether you can commit to showing up for the season, not whether you'd like to. If your shifts are unpredictable or you're this wrecked after a normal day, saying yes and then missing weeks is worse for Mateo than saying no now — and it's fine to tell him exactly that: "I want in, but I can't promise I'll make most weeks with my hours. Save the spot for someone who can, and I'll sub when I'm free."

If you do want to try, the low-risk move is to ask him whether the league takes subs or has a drop-in night, so you're not holding a roster spot you can't fill.

On Toby and the guys — one round of photos isn't enough to conclude much. It could be a standing group thing you've drifted out of, or it could be a trip that got organized in a thread you're not in. If you want to know, the direct route works better than reading the feed: text Toby something plain like "saw the Chelan pics — looks great. Was that a standing thing? I'd be up for the next one." His answer tells you more than the pictures did.

What's your read on whether you actually want the bowling league, versus feeling like you should want it?

I hear what you're saying about not jumping to conclusions, but it's not like Toby's phone broke. They planned that trip over weeks. I saw the photos—same three guys who've been in the group chat since junior year. No invite, no heads up. Feels pretty clear.

Fair — I'll take that. A multi-week trip with the same three guys from a chat you're in, and no mention of it, is different from a stray photo. That's not you reading tea leaves; that's a pattern with a shape to it. I was wrong to file it under "one round of photos."

What it establishes: they organized something without you, and nobody flagged it. What it doesn't establish is why. Exclusion on purpose, drift, someone assuming you'd be working and couldn't come, a smaller trip that grew — those all look identical from the outside. You don't have to solve that to decide what you do next, but it does change the move.

Given the chat is shared and the trip was weeks in the making, the direct question is still the right one, just less soft than I framed it: "Chelan looked great. Was there a reason I wasn't in on it?" That's not fishing. It's asking a group you've been in since junior year to account for something. Their answer — or the way they dodge it — is the actual information.

And it's worth separating two things: whether you want to keep investing in that group, and whether you want the bowling league. They're not the same decision, and you don't have to resolve the first one to answer the second by Wednesday.

You're wrecked and it's late. Nothing here needs to be settled tonight.
I get what you're saying. But real friends don't make you apply to hang out. If they wanted me there, they'd have said something. Silence is its own answer.

There's truth in that, and I'm not going to talk you out of it. If you've been in that chat since junior year and a weeks-long trip came together without a word to you, the silence is data. You're not obligated to chase an invitation that never came, and "real friends don't make you apply" is a defensible line to hold.

Where I'd push back is on treating the silence as a complete verdict. It's a real signal about how the group is functioning right now — but it's still compatible with a few different stories, and the difference matters for what you do with it. If it's drift, the friendship may be winding down on their end and you get to decide whether to let it. If it's something specific — a misread, an assumption you were working, someone else driving the planning — that's fixable, but only if someone says something. The silence tells you they didn't include you. It doesn't tell you they decided against you.

So the honest version: you don't owe them a request to be included. You also don't have to write them off tonight to protect yourself from it. You can let it sit, put your energy where it's returned, and see whether anyone reaches out on their own. That's not applying. That's just not doing their work for them.

The thing with a Wednesday deadline is that it's a decision you can actually make. The group thing isn't on a clock. Don't let the sting from one push you into a call on the other.

I saw you said the silence doesn't tell me they decided against me. But that's kind of the same thing when nobody bothers to reach out after knowing you for six years. Wednesday's the drop deadline. I don't want to let Mateo down, but man, I can barely keep my eyes open past 8 PM most nights.

I'll hold the line I drew, because it's the accurate one: six years of history and no reach-out is a strong signal that the group isn't prioritizing you right now. That's real, and it's worth taking seriously. What it still isn't is proof of a decision against you — nobody in that chat has said a word either way, and you'd be filling in the motive yourself. That distinction isn't me softening it. It's the difference between "they've drifted" and "they chose to cut me," and you don't actually know which one it is.

But here's the thing — you don't need to resolve that to answer the question that's actually on a clock.

On Mateo: you already told me the real constraint. Ten-hour shifts, wrecked, asleep by 8 most nights. That's not a motivation problem, it's a capacity problem, and no amount of wanting to be there fixes it. Signing up for a season you can't show up to isn't loyalty to Mateo — it's a spot he could've given someone who'd actually be on the lanes, plus a string of no-shows he has to explain. That's the version that lets him down.

The move that respects both of you is to tell him the truth before Wednesday: "I want in, but my hours are killing me and I can't commit to most weeks. Don't hold a spot for me — but if you ever need a sub, call me and I'll come when I can." That's not dropping out. That's being straight with him, which is more than the group chat is doing for you.

You're running on empty and it's late. The Mateo text is one message. Send it tomorrow, not tonight.

I just scrolled back through the group chat to check. There's a poll from two weeks ago asking about Chelan dates. I didn't see it because my phone was muted during my apprenticeship exam prep. The notifications got buried under study group messages.

That changes it, and I want to be straight about that rather than quietly sliding past it. You went back and looked instead of staying with the conclusion, and what you found is a poll you missed — not a decision made without you. That's the difference between the two stories I kept saying were possible, and now you have the answer. They asked. You didn't see it.

So the "silence is its own answer" read doesn't hold up. It wasn't silence aimed at you; it was a notification you never got, buried under exam prep. That's a much more ordinary thing, and it's worth saying plainly: they didn't cut you out.

What I'd do with it: post in the chat, no drama, something like "Just saw the Chelan poll — my phone was buried in exam prep and I missed it. Looks like a good trip. Count me in for the next one." That closes the loop without making anyone apologize for something they didn't do, and it puts you back in the thread where the next plan will happen.

One practical note, since this is the second time a buried notification has cost you something: the group chat is where plans live, and muting it during a heavy stretch is exactly when you'll miss them. Worth a quick pass through it once a week, or unmuting just that thread.

Now — Mateo. That one's still real, and it's still Wednesday. The exam-prep explanation doesn't change your hours. If you can't make most weeks, the sub offer is still the honest move. But you might check whether the league runs a shorter season or a sub list before you decide you're out entirely.

You did the right thing scrolling back. That's the part that actually resolved this.
